source_note: Official Stanford course page https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs186/ (CS 186 / PHIL 86, 'How to make a moral agent', Spring 2026, Jared Moore & David Gottlieb) — schedule of dated sessions with lecture titles and attached readings; fetched 2026-10-21.

lectures.title: Agents and Moral Agents
lectures.summary: First session of the course, introducing the distinction between agents and moral agents that frames its question of whether AI systems can be moral agents.

lectures.title: Agents and Moral Agents
lectures.summary: Second session on agents and moral agents; the assigned reading is Peter Railton's 'Ethical Learning, Natural and Artificial', and a page note says Railton may visit the class.

lectures.title: Moral Sentimentalism
lectures.summary: Introduces moral sentimentalism through the primary texts of its classic proponents: Adam Smith's The Theory of Moral Sentiments and Hume's A Treatise of Human Nature.

lectures.title: Moral Sentimentalism
lectures.summary: Continues the sentimentalism unit with Bernard Williams's 'Internal and External Reasons' as the assigned reading; the course project proposal is due this session.

lectures.title: Moral Rationalism
lectures.summary: Introduces moral rationalism through Kant's Groundwork for the Metaphysics of Morals as the assigned reading.

lectures.title: Moral Rationalism
lectures.summary: Continues the rationalism unit with Christine Korsgaard's The Sources of Normativity as the assigned reading.

lectures.title: Identity and Self
lectures.summary: Considers identity and the self through Derek Parfit's Reasons and Persons as the assigned reading.

lectures.title: What makes us so righteous?
lectures.summary: Opens the unit on the origins of morality, with Brian Skyrms's The Stag Hunt and the Evolution of Social Structure and Ken Binmore's Natural Justice as assigned readings.

lectures.title: What makes us so righteous?
lectures.summary: Continues the unit with chapter 2 of Joshua Greene's Moral Tribes: Emotion, Reason, and the Gap Between Us and Them as the assigned reading.

lectures.title: What makes us so righteous?
lectures.summary: Continues the unit with Michael Tomasello's A Natural History of Human Morality (chapters 1, 2 skimmed, and 3) as the assigned reading.

lectures.title: If it's bad that my AI lies, is it bad if I turn it off?
lectures.summary: Opens the AI welfare unit with Robert Long et al.'s 'Taking AI Welfare Seriously' as the assigned reading; a page note says Rob Long visits the class, and the course project draft is due.

lectures.title: If it's bad that my AI lies, is it bad if I turn it off?
lectures.summary: Continues the unit with Peter Godfrey-Smith's 'Mind, Matter, and Metabolism' and Rosa Cao et al.'s 'Why biological naturalism? Because consciousness requires having your own good' as assigned readings.

lectures.title: How to make a moral agent?
lectures.summary: Begins the unit on building moral agents, with Julia Haas et al.'s 'A roadmap for evaluating moral competence in large language models' as the assigned reading.

lectures.title: How to make a moral agent?
lectures.summary: Surveys empirical studies of machine moral judgement through assigned readings on the moral beliefs encoded in LLMs (Scherrer et al.), cooperation in a society of LLM agents (Piatti et al.), the Delphi experiment on machine moral judgement (Jiang et al.), and AI's perceived moral expertise (Dillion et al.), among others.

lectures.title: Alignment
lectures.summary: Introduces AI alignment through chapter 5 ('Value Alignment') of Gabriel et al.'s The Ethics of Advanced AI Assistants, Nick Tarleton's 'Coherent Extrapolated Volition: A Meta-Level Approach to Machine Ethics', and Paul Christiano's 'Clarifying "AI alignment"'.

lectures.title: Alignment
lectures.summary: Continues the alignment unit with Joel Z. Leibo et al.'s 'A theory of appropriateness with applications to generative artificial intelligence' as the assigned reading.

lectures.title: Project work day
lectures.summary: A work session for the course projects rather than a teaching session; no readings or new material are listed.

lectures.title: Project Presentations
lectures.summary: Student course project presentations, under the closing 'Where are we going?' unit.

lectures.title: Project Presentations
lectures.summary: Student course project presentations in the final session of the course.
